reading.title: The Rise of Solar Energy
reading.text: Solar energy has become one of the most promising renewable energy sources in the world. Unlike fossil fuels, which release harmful carbon emissions, solar panels convert sunlight directly into electricity without pollution. The first practical solar cell was invented in 1954 by Bell Laboratories. Today, solar farms cover thousands of acres in countries like China, India, and the United States. One challenge remains: solar panels only produce electricity during daylight hours. To overcome this, engineers are developing better batteries to store excess energy for use at night. In the future, solar power may become the world's primary energy source.

reading.title: The Great Library of Alexandria
reading.text: The Great Library of Alexandria was one of the largest and most significant libraries of the ancient world. Founded in the 3rd century BCE in Egypt, it aimed to collect all the world's knowledge. Scholars from around the Mediterranean came to study its vast collection of scrolls, estimated at 400,000 to 700,000 texts. Unfortunately, the library was destroyed over several centuries by fires and invasions. Its loss is considered one of the greatest intellectual tragedies in history. Today, the Bibliotheca Alexandrina, a modern library, stands near its original site, honoring the legacy of the ancient library.

reading.title: The Science of Soap Bubbles
reading.text: Soap bubbles may seem like simple children's toys, but they are actually fascinating scientific objects. A bubble consists of a thin film of soapy water surrounding air. The film has three layers: a layer of water molecules between two layers of soap molecules. When light hits the bubble, it reflects off both the outer and inner surfaces, creating the colorful interference patterns we see. Bubbles always form spheres because the sphere is the shape with the smallest surface area for a given volume. Scientists have studied bubbles to understand problems in physics, chemistry, and even medicine.
